title: Distinct Subsequences
prompt: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return the number of distinct subsequences of `s` which equal `t`. A subsequence is formed by deleting some (possibly zero) characters of `s` without disturbing the relative order of the remaining characters.

examples.explanation: There are 3 ways to remove one of the three 'b's from "rabbbit" to leave "rabbit".

constraints: s and t consist of English letters
hints: Think about matching s and t from the end: for the last character of t, you either use the last character of s to match it (if they're equal) or you skip the last character of s entirely.
Define dp[i][j] as the number of ways s[0:i] forms t[0:j] as a subsequence. dp[i][0] = 1 for all i (the empty target is always achieved exactly once, by deleting everything).

If s[i-1] == t[j-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] (use this character to match) + dp[i-1][j] (skip it, hoping earlier characters of s still form t[0:j]). If they differ, only the skip option applies: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j].

solution.approach: Define dp[i][j] as the number of distinct subsequences of s[0:i] equal to t[0:j]. Base case dp[i][0] = 1 for every i, since deleting all of s[0:i] always produces the empty string exactly one way. When s[i-1] == t[j-1], there are two ways to extend a match: use s[i-1] to match t[j-1] (contributing dp[i-1][j-1] ways to match the rest) or skip s[i-1] entirely and still try to match all of t[0:j] using only s[0:i-1] (contributing dp[i-1][j] ways) — these are added since both are valid distinct subsequence choices. When the characters differ, s[i-1] cannot contribute to matching t[j-1], so the only option is to skip it: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]. The answer is dp[len(s)][len(t)].
